title: What is Cognitive Load? Why Does it Matter?
author: The Science of Explanation
summary: Using the everyday scenario of deciphering a prescription label, the piece introduces cognitive load theory by distinguishing two sources of mental strain: intrinsic complexity (how hard the subject itself is, relative to what the learner already knows) and extraneous load (how badly the information is presented, independent of its actual difficulty). It explains working memory through the metaphor of a truck with a limited carrying capacity, and connects load directly to 'chunking' -- the mind's strategy of compressing detailed information into manageable units -- arguing that when cognitive load is too high, working memory has no spare capacity left to form the new chunks that constitute real learning. A key move in the piece is showing that existing knowledge lowers load by supplying ready-made chunks: a physicist reading a dark-matter paper experiences far less load than a layperson because their trained schema does the compressing automatically. The piece closes with a practical framework for communicators and teachers: manage the intrinsic complexity of what you're explaining relative to the audience's existing knowledge, and strip out any extraneous load that consumes working memory without contributing to understanding.
points: Distinguishes intrinsic load (complexity inherent to the subject relative to the learner's prior knowledge) from extraneous load (difficulty added purely by poor presentation) as two separate levers teachers can manage independently.

Uses the 'chunking' concept to explain why overloaded working memory doesn't just feel effortful -- it actively prevents new long-term memory structures from forming, so information that never becomes a 'chunk' is effectively not learned.

Argues that expertise functions as a load-reduction mechanism: existing chunks let an expert compress and connect new information automatically, which is why the same material can be low-load for one reader and impossibly dense for another.

Reduces good explanation to two disciplined moves: calibrate complexity to what the audience already knows, and ruthlessly remove any extraneous load that competes for working-memory resources without aiding comprehension.
quotes: The first is the complexity of the subject. A new prescription comes with complexity that's intrinsic to the task. You'll need to understand instructions, dosage, schedules, and refills.
Think of working memory as a truck that can carry a limited load. If the load is bigger than the capacity, things start to fall off. The same is true with the mind.

The problem is that chunking requires free working memory. If the mind is under pressure due to complexity, there aren't enough free resources for creating new chunks. So we read a dense scientific paper, but don't remember any of it.

In this example, the existing chunks of the nuclear physicist helped reduce the cognitive pressure and free up working memory. This is why what an audience already knows matters as much as what you're trying to teach them.
Intrinsic load: Complexity is all around us. This load represents how much processing is required to grasp the complexity of a subject, relative to the learner's existing knowledge.
The lesson: Manage the complexity of the subject you're communicating and make the presentation easier to consume.
